title: Stacks of Coins
statement: A game starts with a single stack of $30$ coins. Each move is one of two kinds. In a split, exactly $3$ coins are taken away from one stack and the rest of that stack is divided into two non-empty stacks. In a join, two stacks are combined into one stack and exactly $1$ new coin is added to it. After some number of moves, there are exactly $6$ stacks containing $11$ coins in total. How many moves have been made?
hints: Ignore the sizes of the individual stacks. Keep track of just two numbers: how many stacks there are and how many coins there are in total. What does each kind of move do to these two numbers?

A split always adds $1$ stack and removes $3$ coins, while a join always removes $1$ stack and adds $1$ coin. Let $s$ be the number of splits and $j$ the number of joins, then set up a pair of simultaneous equations by comparing the start and the end.

The stack count goes from $1$ to $6$, so $s - j = 5$. The coin count goes from $30$ to $11$, so $3s - j = 19$. Subtracting the first equation from the second gives $2s = 14$, so $s = 7$. Now find $j$ and work out what the question asks for.
solution: Each kind of move changes the number of stacks and the total number of coins by a fixed amount, whichever stacks are used. A split replaces one stack by two, so the number of stacks rises by $1$, and the total number of coins falls by $3$. A join replaces two stacks by one, so the number of stacks falls by $1$, and the total number of coins rises by $1$. Suppose that $s$ splits and $j$ joins have been made, in any order. The number of stacks goes from $1$ to $6$, so $1 + s - j = 6$, which gives $s - j = 5$. The number of coins goes from $30$ to $11$, so $30 - 3s + j = 11$, which gives $3s - j = 19$. Subtracting the first equation from the second removes $j$ and leaves $2s = 14$. So $s = 7$, and then $j = s - 5 = 2$. Any game ending in this position therefore has exactly $7 + 2 = 9$ moves. Such a game does exist. Seven splits, each cutting off a stack of $1$, take the large stack through $30, 26, 22, 18, 14, 10, 6, 2$, leaving seven stacks of $1$ and one stack of $2$. Two joins, each combining two stacks of $1$ into a stack of $3$, then leave the stacks $1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3$. These are $6$ stacks containing $11$ coins. The number of moves made is $9$. Why this works. linear-system-solving, linear-combination-of-equations: each kind of move has a fixed effect on the two totals, so the numbers of splits and joins satisfy two linear equations, and subtracting them eliminates the joins.
